rv.q: A heady production with stellar performances, Rapture is a thriller, a trickster, and an absolute romp.

Kirkwood's layered text relentlessly challenges the audience to assess our own engagement with the piece, raising troubling questions about how we assess information, what sources we trust, and how much of what we're told we are prepared to believe.
This is ambitious, richly allusive, endlessly debatable theatre.
On its own merits the play is an enjoyably slippery, enthralling piece of work, albeit with a tiresome metatheatrical framework.
Cut by three-quarters of an hour and discover a masterpiece.
But for all that, it's hampered by its own elusiveness.
Is this play good enough to overshadow all the drama? Kinda.
After all the hype, a damp squib for the silly season.
The whole set-up is completely phoney and the most real thing in the show is a scene during lockdown in which the couple wash their groceries.
Kirkwood and the director Lucy Morrison utterly fail to generate any sort of tension.
For my part, I was not just swept along but also moved and at times genuinely shaken by the startling anger underpinning an (apparent!) tragedy.
Working together, the writer and director Lucy Morrison make thrilling theatre.
It is a contrived piece that lasts non-stop for 1 hour 45 minutes with no interval but it engaged me the whole time.
This is a funny, sweet-natured marital comedy with a powerful anti-lockdown message.
Much of the rest of the play feels taken up by the feat of its mismarketing and duty as a documenting exercise, but not in a way which yields anything of destabilising depth or surprise.
It's a mildly amusing comedy of manners trapped in a desperate attempt to be exciting.

What follows is a piece of dramatised reportage which all but accuses this country’s establishment of murdering those it deems to be a threat, in this case ordinary couple Noah and Celeste, who became activists for social change. If I tell you more I may risk putting myself in the crosshairs of these same dark forces.
For those who think it stays just on the clever side, it succeeds in being an incredibly interesting piece of theatre, one you'll be thinking and talking about long after.
Kirkwood's play still works on many levels, particularly the one that forces us to question our most trusted sources of information.

cn.t: Kirkwood's meta-theatrical hoax divides critics: some praise its clever commentary on truth and surveillance, while others dismiss the gimmick as annoying and the underlying thriller as underwhelming.
